newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian race row politician raises Asian concerns.
newsitem.headline: Australian race row politician raises Asian concerns.

text.p: Some of Asia's top business leaders believe Australian race row politician Pauline Hanson is harming Australia-Asia trade, according to a newspaper poll published on Monday.
But Australian business chiefs dismissed the survey's negative findings, saying Asians were pragmatic and realised that Hanson, an independent politician, was a "one-man band".
The survey of 200 business leaders in Kuala Lumpur, Manila, Bangkok and Jakarta, found six to seven percent said they were now less likely to do business with Australian companies.
This compared with 84 percent who said Australia was still a "favourable" or "very favourable" destination for business, The Sydney Morning Herald reported.

Australia-Asia business chambers on Monday highlighted the positive side of the poll, which surveyed senior managers from top-500 companies in each Asian city, but conceded that Asia was concerned about Hanson.
"It (Hanson) is obviously a concern and it's raised regularly in Australia-Malaysia business meetings," said John Westmacott, spokesman for the Australia-Malaysia Chamber of Commerce.
"But I do not think it is affecting the conduct of business," Westmacott told Reuters.

The newspaper survey also found that 25 percent of the Asian business leaders immediately recognised the name Hanson, compared with only five percent who recognised Australian Prime Minister John Howard without being prompted.
Paul Gallagher, executive director of the South East Asia Business Councils, said Asian awareness of Hanson was fuelled by the extensive media coverage given to her in the region.

"Certainly there is an awareness of Hanson because Asian media have given coverage to the whole Hanson debate, but overall there is still a very positive reaction to Australia," Gallagher told Reuters.
"From the first-hand experience of many Asian leaders they know that there is not a general racist attitude here in Australia," Gallagher said.
The survey also found a concern among some Asian business leaders towards visiting Australia, which has been engulfed in a bitter race debate since September 1996.

One Jakarta business leader told the newspaper: "I know for a fact that throughout Southeast Asia many people have concluded after reading the coverage that Australians are racist towards Asians. They now feel it is more dangerous for Asians to visit".

But the survey found that 88 percent of respondents thought Australia was a "favourable" or "very favourable" holiday destination. In the year to May 1997, Asian tourists numbers rose 11.2 percent to 1.3 million, excluding Japanese.
Independent politician Hanson sparked a bitter race debate in Australia last September when she made her maiden speech to parliament, claiming Australia was being swamped by Asians.
Hanson's newly-registered One Nation party, which has a platform of anti-immigration and anti-Aborginal welfare, has attracted rowdy and and at times violent protests.
Opinion polls show support for Hanson in Australia ranging between six and 10 percent.
